intake_responses.competitors: This whole section of Owino is shoes, maybe 50 other vendors. Some have connections to get better bales, others sell new Chinese shoes which are taking our customers.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make profit from marking up shoes, buying a pair at 15,000 and selling at 25,000 or 30,000. During back-to-school season, I can make up to 2 million shillings profit monthly.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Market authorities keep threatening to relocate us but won't say where or when, making it hard to invest in improving my stall. How can I expand when I don't know if I'll be here next month?
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm saving to rent a small shop outside the market as backup. Also teaching my daughter the business so she can help me manage if we have to operate in two locations.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a juice processing unit making passion fruit, mango and pineapple juice. We package in 300ml and 500ml bottles and supply to schools and supermarkets around Mbarara.
intake_responses.customers: Schools are my biggest customers, especially boarding schools that buy in bulk. Also supply to local supermarkets and sometimes get orders for events like weddings.
intake_responses.competitors: Splash, Cheers and other big brands dominate supermarkets. Local processors like me struggle because customers trust big brands more even if our juice is fresher.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Selling juice to institutions brings steady income, about 5-7 million monthly. Event orders are irregular but profitable, can make 2 million from one big wedding.
intake_responses.main_challenge: UNBS standards keep changing and each adjustment means buying new equipment or changing our process. Last month they said our labels need new information which means reprinting thousands of labels I already bought.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to get UNBS certification for our facility which might reduce surprise inspections. Also planning to start a farm to grow our own fruits and control quality better.

intake_responses.business_description: I develop mobile apps and websites for SMEs, been doing this for 3 years since graduating from Makerere. I work with two other developers on a project basis.
intake_responses.customers: Small businesses wanting online presence, NGOs needing data collection apps, and startups with app ideas but no technical skills. Most clients come through referrals.
intake_responses.competitors: Many freelance developers and small tech companies in Kampala. Indian companies also compete online offering very low prices that we can't match.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Project fees range from 500,000 for simple websites to 10 million for complex apps. Also make recurring income from maintenance contracts, about 200,000 per client monthly.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Clients disappear after paying deposit, then resurface months later wanting urgent completion but the technology has changed. Keeping up with new frameworks while managing old projects is exhausting and expensive.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm creating standard packages with clear timelines and expiry dates for deposits. Also investing in online courses to keep skills current and maybe specialize in one technology stack.

intake_responses.business_description: I grow oranges on 20 acres and also buy from other farmers to supply markets in Kampala. During peak season I send two trucks weekly to Nakasero and Kalerwe markets.
intake_responses.customers: Juice makers in Kampala, retail traders in markets, and sometimes export traders who take oranges to South Sudan. Hotels and restaurants also buy directly from me.
intake_responses.competitors: Other orange traders from Soroti and Teso region, plus those bringing oranges from Tanzania. The Tanzanian oranges look better even if ours taste sweeter.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Selling oranges in bulk to Kampala markets, making about 300,000 to 500,000 profit per truck. My own harvest brings better margins than buying from others.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Transport costs have doubled but market prices haven't increased proportionally. Fuel prices, truck maintenance, and police checkpoints all eat into profits making some trips barely worthwhile.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm organizing other farmers to hire trucks together and share costs. Also exploring value addition like making concentrated juice that's easier to transport than fresh oranges.

intake_responses.business_description: I import and sell curtains, bedsheets, and home decorations from Dubai and China. My shop in Kikuubo has been operating for 6 years and I employ 3 sales girls.
intake_responses.customers: Interior designers, hotels refurbishing, newlyweds setting up homes, and retailers from upcountry who buy wholesale. Chinese New Year affects our business heavily.
intake_responses.competitors: Many shops in Kikuubo sell similar items, maybe 20 on this arcade alone. Container traders who import directly sell cheaper but don't give customers variety like specialized shops.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Retail sales with 40-60% markup on landed cost. Wholesale orders to upcountry traders bring volume but lower margins, about 20% profit.
intake_responses.main_challenge: The landlord keeps increasing rent claiming dollar inflation but won't accept payment in dollars. Monthly rent jumped from 2.5 million to 4 million in just one year making it hard to maintain profits.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm negotiating with other tenants to approach the landlord as a group. Also looking at opening an online store to reduce dependency on this expensive physical location.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a digital marketing agency helping Jinja businesses with social media, websites and online advertising. Started 2 years ago after leaving my bank job.
intake_responses.customers: Hotels and lodges around Jinja, restaurants, tour companies and some manufacturers. Recently getting clients from Kampala who want cheaper services than capital agencies.
intake_responses.competitors: Kampala agencies taking Jinja clients, freelancers undercutting prices, and DIY business owners using Canva. Many clients don't see value in professional marketing.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Monthly retainer fees from social media management, ranging from 300,000 to 1 million per client. One-off projects like websites bring in 2-5 million each.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Clients expect instant results like immediate sales from Facebook posts but don't understand marketing is long-term. They cancel contracts after one month claiming no ROI which disrupts cash flow.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm developing case studies with metrics to show value better. Also shifting to performance-based pricing where part of payment depends on reaching agreed targets.

intake_responses.business_description: I make and supply pancakes to schools and tea shops around Fort Portal. Started with one sigiri, now I have a full kitchen and employ 4 people including delivery riders.
intake_responses.customers: Schools order every morning for break time, tea shops stock for their customers, and events like conferences and weddings. Morning hours are crazy busy for us.
intake_responses.competitors: Several home-based pancake makers and bakeries that also make pancakes. Some schools started making their own to cut costs which reduced our market.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Selling pancakes at 500-1000 shillings each depending on size and ingredients. Schools order 200-500 pieces daily, bringing in about 4-6 million monthly during term time.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Maintaining consistent taste when scaling up is harder than I thought. Customers complain that pancakes taste different from batch to batch, but training new cooks to match my standards takes forever.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm documenting exact recipes and processes, even recording videos for training. Want to also diversify into other snacks so we're not dependent only on pancakes.

intake_responses.business_description: I operate a driving school with 5 cars and 8 instructors. We teach all classes of driving from motorcycles to trucks, been in business for 5 years now.
intake_responses.customers: Youth wanting to become commercial drivers, company drivers needing license upgrades, and bodaboda riders getting permits. NGO training programs also bring bulk students.
intake_responses.competitors: Three other driving schools in Mbale town, plus briefcase operators who use one car and charge very low fees. Traffic police also recommend specific schools which affects fair competition.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Training fees range from 250,000 for motorcycle to 800,000 for truck licenses. Refresher courses and license renewal assistance bring additional income.
intake_responses.main_challenge: The new traffic regulations require computerized testing but the system keeps failing during exams. Students fail not because of skills but technical glitches, damaging our reputation when they blame us.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm partnering with a school in Kampala that has better connections at the licensing office. Also investing in a simulator to give students practice with computerized systems.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell kitchenware and plastics in Lira main market. Plates, cups, buckets, basins, jerrycans, everything for the home, I've been here 12 years.
intake_responses.customers: Housewives shopping for their homes, restaurants buying in bulk, and village traders who come to stock their small shops. Market days Wednesday and Saturday are busiest.
intake_responses.competitors: About 15 other stalls selling similar items in this market. The Chinese shop that opened in town sells cheaper plastics though they break easily.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make 30-50% markup on wholesale prices from Kampala. Good months especially December I can make 3 million profit, slow months maybe 800,000.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Fake products are flooding the market and customers can't tell the difference until items break. When they come back complaining, I've already sold my stock and can't trace the supplier.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm building relationships with trusted suppliers who guarantee quality. Also educating customers on identifying genuine products by checking certain marks and thickness.

intake_responses.business_description: I run an urban farming venture growing vegetables using hydroponics in Kalerwe. We supply fresh lettuce, tomatoes and cucumbers to hotels and supermarkets.
intake_responses.customers: High-end hotels in Kampala want consistent quality vegetables, supermarkets like Capital Shoppers and Carrefour, and some restaurants in Kololo. They pay premium for pesticide-free produce.
intake_responses.competitors: Traditional farmers sell cheaper but inconsistent quality. Other urban farmers are coming up but few do hydroponics properly so quality varies.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Selling premium vegetables at 3-4 times regular market price. Monthly revenue around 8-12 million depending on harvest cycles and client orders.
intake_responses.main_challenge: The greenhouse materials deteriorate quickly in our weather but replacements are expensive. UV sheets that should last 4 years barely make it to 2 years, forcing unplanned capital expenses.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm researching local alternatives for greenhouse covering and talking to Kacita to import directly. Also planning a demo farm where clients can see our methods and build trust.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell children's clothes both new and second-hand in Owino. I import new clothes from Turkey and also buy bales of used clothes from Container Village.
intake_responses.customers: Parents shopping for their kids, especially during back-to-school season. Also get bulk buyers who resell in villages and refugee settlements.
intake_responses.competitors: This section has maybe 100 stalls selling children's wear. Online sellers on Facebook and WhatsApp are taking customers who don't want to come to crowded Owino.
intake_responses.revenue_source: New clothes have 100% markup while second-hand gives 200-300% profit. I make 3-5 million monthly, but January after school shopping can hit 10 million.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Balancing inventory between new and used clothes is tricky because customer preferences shift unpredictably. Sometimes I'm stuck with expensive Turkish stock while customers only want second-hand.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm analyzing sales patterns from last two years to predict better. Also started a WhatsApp catalog to presell items before importing, reducing risk of dead stock.

intake_responses.business_description: I process and package groundnut paste, sim sim paste and local cooking oil. My factory employs 12 people and we supply shops across Northern Uganda.
intake_responses.customers: Supermarkets in Gulu, Kitgum and Lira stock our products. Schools buy cooking oil in bulk, and households buy our groundnut paste for making sauce.
intake_responses.competitors: Mukwano and other big brands dominate supermarkets. Local processors sell unpackaged products cheaper in markets making it hard to compete on price.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Groundnut paste sales bring in about 60% of revenue, cooking oil 30%, and sim sim paste 10%. Monthly turnover is around 15-20 million shillings.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Power outages damage our machines and spoil products in process, but backup generators consume too much fuel. Some days we lose 2 million worth of groundnuts because power cut during roasting.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm investing in solar power system though initial cost is high. Also negotiating with Umeme for industrial connection which has more stable supply than commercial lines.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a motorcycle spare parts shop here in Kikuubo, been doing this for 4 years now. We stock parts for bajaj, TVS, and all the common boda boda brands you see around town.
intake_responses.customers: My main customers are boda boda riders and mechanics from around Kampala, some even come from Mukono and Wakiso. Most of them know me personally and buy on credit which I allow for my regulars.
intake_responses.competitors: There are maybe 15 other spare parts dealers just on this street alone, but I try to keep genuine parts unlike others. The Chinese shops are really cutting into our market with cheaper parts.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make money from selling the parts, sometimes I get a markup of 30-40% on genuine parts. During rainy season business is better because bodas break down more often.
intake_responses.main_challenge: The tax authorities are becoming too aggressive with their enforcement and keep changing requirements for small businesses like mine. Last month they wanted me to install EFRIS but the system doesn't work properly with our type of business.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm trying to register properly and comply with all URA requirements but it's confusing. Maybe I need to hire someone who understands these tax systems better than me.

intake_responses.business_description: I started a fresh juice and smoothie bar after campus, targeting health-conscious people and tourists visiting the source of the Nile. We use only fresh fruits from local farmers, no concentrates at all.
intake_responses.customers: Mostly young professionals, tourists from the hotels nearby, and students from Busoga University come here. On weekends we get families who come for the healthy kids' menu I introduced.
intake_responses.competitors: There's Café Javas and other big chains but they're more expensive, then local juice sellers who use water and sugar which I don't. My direct competition is probably two other juice bars that opened recently.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Daily juice sales bring in about 300,000-500,000 UGX, more on weekends and holidays. I also do outside catering for events which can bring 2-3 million per event.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Getting packaging materials that are both eco-friendly and affordable is becoming impossible since the government banned certain plastics. The paper alternatives leak and customers complain but the good ones are too expensive.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm researching biodegradable packaging suppliers from Kenya and testing different materials. Maybe I'll have to increase prices but I'm worried about losing price-sensitive customers.

intake_responses.business_description: I buy sesame seeds, sunflower, and groundnuts from farmers in Acholi sub-region and sell to exporters in Kampala. Been in this business since the war ended, started small but now I handle big volumes.
intake_responses.customers: My buyers are mainly export companies in Kampala like Mount Meru, Olam, and some Indian traders in Lugogo. They want consistent quality and quantity which is hard to guarantee.
intake_responses.competitors: Many middlemen have joined this business now that agriculture is picking up in the north. Some even go directly to villages with trucks which makes farmers bypass us in the markets.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make profit from the margin between buying and selling price, usually 200-400 shillings per kilogram. In a good season I can move 50-100 tons per month.
intake_responses.main_challenge: The moisture content requirements from exporters are becoming stricter but farmers don't have proper drying facilities and rain can spoil everything. I lose a lot of money when shipments are rejected for high moisture.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to set up a central drying facility with a moisture meter but it needs serious capital. For now I'm training farmers on better drying methods and lending them tarpaulins.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a printing and branding business near campus, we do banners, t-shirts, business cards, and promotional materials. Started with one small machine but now we have heat press, large format printer, everything.
intake_responses.customers: Universities and students are our biggest customers, then small businesses, NGOs doing workshops, and political campaigns during election time. We get a lot of rush orders for events and dissertations.
intake_responses.competitors: There are so many printing businesses in Wandegeya now, maybe 20 just on this stretch. Everyone is undercutting prices so profit margins are really squeezed these days.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Printing services bring daily income, but the real money comes from big branding contracts with companies. One vehicle branding job can equal a whole week of small printing jobs.
intake_responses.main_challenge: The cost of servicing and maintaining these Chinese printing machines is killing my profits because technicians who understand them properly are few and charge too much. When a machine breaks, I lose customers to competitors.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm planning to train one of my employees in machine maintenance, maybe send them for a course. Also looking at getting service contracts but they're expensive upfront.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell hardware items like cement, iron sheets, paints, and plumbing materials here in Mbarara market. Started as a porter but saved up and opened my own shop 8 years ago.
intake_responses.customers: Contractors, home builders, and fundis from all over Ankole region come here. Some big customers buy in bulk for construction projects in villages, I even deliver using hired trucks.
intake_responses.competitors: Big hardware shops are opening with Chinese owners who import directly and sell cheaper. Even Steel and Tube opened a branch here so small traders like us are feeling the pressure.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I make profit on markup, especially on small items like nails, paint brushes where customers don't compare prices much. Cement gives small margin but moves fast so it keeps cash flowing.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Customers are demanding tax invoices now but EFRIS system is complicated for someone like me who didn't go far in school and my sales girl doesn't understand it either. URA keeps threatening to close non-compliant businesses.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm looking for a educated person who can help manage the tax system, maybe a university student part-time. But I worry they might steal from me if they understand my business too well.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a computer training center and internet café in Soroti town, teaching basic computer skills, graphics design, and offering internet services. We're the biggest ICT center in Teso sub-region.
intake_responses.customers: Students, job seekers needing to type CVs, NGO workers, and government employees who need computer training. Recently we're getting many teachers because of the new digital curriculum requirements.
intake_responses.competitors: A few small internet cafés exist but none offer proper training like us. The real competition is smartphones because everyone now has internet on their phones so café business is declining.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Training fees bring in about 3-5 million monthly, internet café maybe 1 million, and we do typing and printing services. I also repair computers and phones which adds extra income.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Load shedding in Soroti is terrible and running on generator is too expensive, but without power I lose training hours and internet customers go elsewhere. The power schedule is so unpredictable we can't plan properly.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm saving to invest in a solar backup system but it needs at least 15 million for a good setup. For now I'm trying to negotiate with Umeme for better connection but they don't care about small businesses.

intake_responses.business_description: I operate a pork joint in Kalerwe, we roast pork and serve with cassava, cabbage, the usual local style. Started with just a sigiri but now we have proper roasting ovens and seating for 50 people.
intake_responses.customers: Mainly local residents, market vendors, and people working in garages around Kalerwe. On weekends we get people from all over Kampala who know our pork is the best, some even take away for parties.
intake_responses.competitors: Every corner in Kalerwe has a pork joint now, maybe 30 in this area alone. The competition is crazy and everyone is copying each other, even stealing workers who know recipes.
intake_responses.revenue_source: We sell pork by the kilogram, usually 25,000-30,000 per kg depending on the cut. Beer sales also bring good money, sometimes more than the food because markup is better.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Health inspectors and KCCA enforcement are becoming too strict, wanting licenses and certificates that cost millions yet they don't help us improve anything. They just come to collect money or threaten closure.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm trying to formalize everything, get all required licenses and meet health standards. But the requirements keep changing and the process is frustrating, maybe I need to join the restaurant association.

intake_responses.business_description: I sell ladies' shoes and handbags in Mbale town, I import from Dubai and Turkey through dealers in Kampala. My shop is small but I stock unique designs you won't find in other shops here.
intake_responses.customers: Young women, especially working class and campus girls from Islamic University who want trendy items. During graduation season and December holidays, business really picks up as people want new things.
intake_responses.competitors: The Chinese shops sell similar items much cheaper but quality is poor. My challenge is other traders who go to Kampala and bring one or two pieces of what I'm selling, spoiling the exclusivity.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I usually mark up 100-150% on landed cost, so a shoe that costs me 40,000 I sell at 80,000-100,000. During peak season I can make 5-8 million profit per month.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Currency fluctuation affects my business badly because I buy in dollars but customers are paying less in shillings now that dollar is high. I can't increase prices too much or they'll go to cheaper shops.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm trying to buy more during low dollar periods and stock up, but that ties up capital. Also exploring local suppliers who make quality shoes but designs aren't as trendy as imports.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a tours and travel company specializing in trips to national parks around Fort Portal like Kibale, Queen Elizabeth, and mountain climbing. We handle both local and international tourists, providing full packages.
intake_responses.customers: International tourists from booking sites, local schools organizing trips, and corporate groups doing team building. Chinese and Indian tourists are increasing lately, they like Rwenzori mountains.
intake_responses.competitors: Many brief case companies have joined tourism, they undercut prices and provide poor service which spoils the market. Established companies in Kampala also take most international bookings.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Commission from hotels, park fees markup, transport charges, and guide fees. A good tourist group can bring in 10-20 million profit, but seasons are very unpredictable now.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Maintaining service quality when using freelance guides and drivers is hard because good ones are poached by bigger companies or start their own operations. Training new ones is expensive and they leave anyway.
intake_responses.current_plan: I want to employ permanent staff but it's costly during low season. For now I'm creating contracts with penalties for guides who abandon trips and building relationships so they stay loyal.

intake_responses.business_description: I run a grain milling business in Lira town, we mill maize, millet, cassava into flour. I have three diesel mills and employ 5 people, we serve the whole district and even parts of Apac.
intake_responses.customers: Local people bring their grains for milling, schools buy flour in bulk, and some traders who package and resell in Kampala. During harvest season we operate almost 24 hours because of demand.
intake_responses.competitors: Many small mills have opened in villages with government support so people don't come to town as much. Electric mills in town charge less because they don't buy diesel like us.
intake_responses.revenue_source: We charge per basin or per sack for milling services, and we buy grain to mill and sell as flour with better margin. The flour business is more profitable than just service milling.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Diesel prices keep rising and we can't increase milling charges too much because customers will go to electric mills, but electricity isn't reliable enough for me to convert. Generator power is even more expensive than diesel engines.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm exploring hybrid system where I can use electricity when available and diesel as backup. The conversion cost is high but might save money long-term if I get a loan.

intake_responses.business_description: I deal in secondhand electronics like TVs, radios, home theaters from Owino market, been here 12 years. We test everything before selling and give one month guarantee which most traders don't do.
intake_responses.customers: People looking for affordable electronics, students going to campus, small hotels and bars needing TVs. Many customers are from upcountry who trust Owino for variety and prices.
intake_responses.competitors: Now everyone is selling electronics, even new Chinese products are almost same price as our quality secondhand. Some traders sell broken items cheap which spoils the market reputation for all of us.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Markup depends on the item condition and brand, usually 30-50% profit on cost. Quick-moving items like small radios have less margin but TVs and decoders give better profit.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Sources of good secondhand electronics are drying up because of competition and Europe is sending less quality items to Africa now. The good stuff is picked at port in Mombasa before reaching us.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm building relationships with clearing agents in Mombasa to get better picks. Also thinking of mixing new cheap items with secondhand to give customers more options.

intake_responses.business_description: I started a digital marketing agency focusing on social media management for SMEs in Jinja and surrounding areas. We handle Facebook, Instagram, and create content for businesses that don't understand online marketing.
intake_responses.customers: Hotels, restaurants, schools, and retail shops in Jinja who want to reach more customers online. Recently we got contracts with some manufacturing companies in the industrial area.
intake_responses.competitors: Kampala agencies sometimes pitch to our clients with fancy proposals but they don't understand local market. Freelancers charge less but don't deliver consistent quality or disappear after being paid.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Monthly retainer fees from clients range from 500,000 to 2 million depending on services. We also make money from one-time projects like logo design and website development.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Clients expect viral content and instant results but don't want to pay for advertising budget or professional photography, they think social media management is just posting. Educating them is exhausting and they blame us when organic reach is low.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm creating case studies from successful campaigns to show value. Also partnering with photographers and influencers to provide complete packages that clients can understand better.

intake_responses.business_description: I run an auto garage in Naalya specializing in Japanese cars, we do general service, engine work, and computerized diagnosis. Most of our mechanics trained in Japan so we understand these cars properly.
intake_responses.customers: Middle class people in Naalya, Kyaliwajjala, Namugongo who drive Toyota, Nissan, Subaru cars. We get referrals because we're honest about problems and don't do unnecessary replacements like other garages.
intake_responses.competitors: Many new garages opening because everyone thinks it's easy money but they lack proper tools and skills. Dealership garages are too expensive so we position ourselves in between with quality service.
intake_responses.revenue_source: Service charges, parts markup (usually 30-40%), and major repairs like engine overhauls that can bring 2-5 million per job. Consistent maintenance customers are the backbone though.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Getting skilled mechanics who won't steal customers or parts is my biggest headache because after training them they either want too much salary or open competing garages nearby. The good ones are poached by dealerships.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm implementing a profit-sharing scheme to keep good mechanics motivated. Also want to start a training program where mechanics sign bonds to work for us for specific periods after training.

intake_responses.business_description: I make and supply mandazi, chapati, and samosas to schools, offices, and events around Gulu. Started with one helper now I have 6 women working with me and we supply over 20 locations daily.
intake_responses.customers: Primary schools for break tea, office canteens, wedding meetings, and small restaurants that don't make their own snacks. During school term business is very steady and predictable.
intake_responses.competitors: Many women are doing this business now but most can't maintain quality when orders are big. Some use poor quality oil and ingredients which I don't compromise on even if profit reduces.
intake_responses.revenue_source: We sell mandazi at 500 shillings each to retailers who sell at 1000, chapati at 1000, samosas 1500. On a good day we can make 400,000-600,000 revenue with about 40% profit after all costs.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Managing working capital is hard because schools want one month credit but I must buy ingredients cash, and when schools delay payment I can't buy materials. Banks don't understand this business to give proper loans.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm negotiating with suppliers for one week credit terms and trying to get more cash-paying customers. Also talking to SACCOs about getting a business loan with easier terms than banks.

intake_responses.business_description: I buy and sell Irish potatoes from Kabale and Kisoro to markets in Mbarara, Masaka, sometimes Kampala. I've been in this business for 20 years, I know all the farmers and market dynamics.
intake_responses.customers: Market vendors, restaurants, schools, and chips makers are my main buyers. I supply consistently so they rely on me even when prices are high during scarcity.
intake_responses.competitors: Many brokers have joined the Irish trade but they disappear when margins are low. The farmers are also trying to sell directly to town but they don't understand market needs like consistent supply.
intake_responses.revenue_source: I buy a sack at maybe 80,000-120,000 from farm and sell at 100,000-150,000 depending on season. Volume is key, I move 200-500 sacks per week so small margins add up.
intake_responses.main_challenge: Price information spreads too fast now with smartphones so farmers know town prices and demand more, killing our margins. But they don't factor transport risks, market fees, and storage losses that we handle.
intake_responses.current_plan: I'm trying to form a traders association to negotiate better with farmers and share transport costs. Also exploring value addition like washing and packaging potatoes for supermarkets.
